paragraphs.text:
Interference occurs when light waves meet and make some places brighter and others dimmer.
Diffraction is the spreading of light waves around edges or through narrow openings.

These effects show that light has wave properties.
But a wave's spreading and its direction of vibration are different things, so we still need to distinguish longitudinal from transverse waves.

The source recounts that Young and Fresnel, pioneers of wave optics, first pictured light as longitudinal waves like sound.
People then imagined an ether filling space and extending inside every object, with light traveling as elastic vibrations in it.

This is an old model from the history of science, not today's explanation of light.
Chapter Four of the source connects transverse elastic vibrations with solids, creating a difficulty for that model.

If the ether behaved like a solid that could support sideways vibrations, it seemed that moving objects should meet resistance.
Such resistance would conflict with the law of inertia, which says that an object keeps its state of motion when no external force acts.

The source says that more and more experimental facts could not be explained by the longitudinal-wave model.
Fresnel therefore accepted that light waves are transverse, although this seemed difficult to understand within the old mechanical-ether model.

Many experiments support the transverse nature of light, and one example uses tourmaline crystals.
The source uses transparent green tourmaline and compares what happens with one crystal and with two.

Tourmaline has a particular crystal axis, and the source calls it a uniaxial crystal.
The rectangular plate in the experiment has one edge aligned with that axis.

In Figure 208, light from a lamp or the Sun falls perpendicular to the plate, as described in the source experiment.
Turning the plate around the beam does not change the transmitted light's intensity, meaning its strength.

The crystal absorbs some light and gives the transmitted light a green tint, so it might seem merely to dim and color the light.
But the transmitted light also gains a new directional property that its brightness alone does not reveal.

A second identical crystal is placed behind the first, with the surfaces of the plates parallel.
When their crystal axes point in the same direction, light still passes, although absorption in the second crystal makes it dimmer, as in Figure 209 a.

With the first crystal fixed, turning the second around the beam gradually dims the transmitted light, as in Figure 209 b.
The light gets weaker as the axes turn from aligned to perpendicular.

At the crossed position in Figure 209 c, the source describes no light getting through because the second crystal absorbs it.
What changes is the relative direction of the crystal axes, not the addition of an ordinary opaque barrier.

The two experiments give two important observations.
First, light from the sources used here has no preferred transverse vibration direction, so rotating the first crystal does not change the transmitted intensity.

Second, the light leaving the first crystal has a particular vibration direction.
Rotating the second crystal therefore changes how much of that light gets through.

In a **longitudinal wave**, vibration is along the direction in which the wave travels.
Sound in air, for example, produces compressions and expansions along that direction.

Turning around the direction of travel gives no different transverse vibration directions to select.
A purely longitudinal-wave model therefore cannot explain the changing transmission when the second crystal turns.

The source explains these experiments with two assumptions.
One describes how light vibrates, and the other describes which vibration directions tourmaline lets through.

The first assumption is that **light waves are transverse, with vibration perpendicular to the direction of travel**.
Figure 210 represents light from an ordinary source, with no single preferred transverse vibration direction.

For light, this vibration means changes in the electric field.
It does not mean that particles of ether move back and forth like a rope.

A transverse wave need not have one fixed transverse vibration direction.
The light considered here can still be symmetric overall around its direction of travel.

For contrast, the source pictures water particles moving in a vertical plane, showing that the water surface gives a particular direction.
This is a simplified picture, not a claim that particles in real water waves only move up and down.

The source calls light with no preferred transverse vibration direction **natural light**.
Here this means **unpolarized light**, whose transverse vibrations are distributed among the possible directions.

Ordinary lamp light and sunlight that has not been changed by another process can be described by this model.
With no preferred direction, rotating the first tourmaline crystal selects the same amount of light each time, so the transmitted intensity stays the same.

The second assumption is that **tourmaline transmits transverse vibration in one particular direction**, lying in plane $p$ in Figure 211.
That plane also contains the direction of travel, while the vibration is perpendicular to the direction of travel.

The transmitted light is called **plane-polarized light**, also known as **linearly polarized light**.
Its electric field changes back and forth along one fixed direction, unlike the unpolarized light called natural light here.

The first crystal makes natural light linearly polarized, so it acts as a **polarizer**.
The second tests the vibration direction of that light, so it acts as an **analyzer**.

When the crystal axes are at $90^\circ$, the analyzer's allowed direction is perpendicular to the incoming vibration direction.
No light passes in the model described by the source.

At an angle other than $90^\circ$, the transmitted vibration amplitude equals the projection of the incoming amplitude onto the second crystal's axis.
A projection keeps the part along that direction, so the analyzer does not simply turn the whole incoming vibration into its own direction.

Tourmaline changes natural light into plane-polarized light, a process called **polarization**.
Polarization selects the direction of transverse vibration, unlike diffraction, which concerns a wave spreading at an opening or edge.

Figure 212 gives a mechanical analogy using a rubber rope and narrow wooden boxes.
A transverse wave travels along the rope while parts of the rope move perpendicular to its length.

The source rapidly changes the direction of this sideways motion to model natural light with no fixed preferred vibration direction.
A narrow opening in the first box restricts the rope's sideways motion to one plane.

The rope wave beyond that box then has a fixed vibration direction, modeling the direction-selecting action of a polarizer.
The rope really moves in this model, but light's electric field is not a rope, and the analogy does not establish an ether.

A second identical box is turned by $90^\circ$ relative to the first.
Its allowed direction of rope motion is then perpendicular to the vibration passed by the first box.

In this model, that vibration cannot pass the second box, leaving no such traveling wave beyond it.
This models crossed crystals blocking transmission, not all motion everywhere in the rope disappearing.

Tourmaline crystals are not the only devices that polarize light, since **polarizing sheets** can do so too.
The source describes an older sheet made with thin crystals of iodoquinine sulfate on celluloid or glass, giving a thickness of 0.1 mm.

That material and thickness are historical details from the source, not the composition and dimensions of every modern polarizing sheet.
The source says these sheets can be used in experiments like those with tourmaline.

It also notes their advantage of polarizing light over a large area rather than only through a small crystal.
For violet light, the source makes the further claim that this material makes violet become white light.

That statement is retained as the source's claim about its material, not as a general rule of polarization.
Selecting a vibration direction does not turn single-color violet light into white light containing many colors.

The source ends with a proposal discussed at the time to reduce glare from oncoming headlights.
It proposed polarizing sheets on both car headlights and windshields.

In that proposal, the sheets would pass vibrations at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal.
The source expected an oncoming car's light to have a vibration direction perpendicular to the direction allowed by the other car's windshield sheet, blocking that light.

It also expected a car's own light to pass through its windshield after reflection from the road.
The source said the proposal would be worthwhile if all cars had the sheets.

These are the source's expectations for the proposal, not a guarantee about light reflected from a real road.
This is a historical proposal, not a recommendation to modify present-day headlights or windshields.
